topics.label: AI Literacy & Capability
topics.description: Critical capabilities needed to become AI fluent — frameworks, competencies, and workforce readiness.

articles.title: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review | npj Digital Public Health - Nature
articles.snippet: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review | npj Digital Public Health  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focuses on European digital public health contexts; findings on competency frameworks may apply to Australian health systems but specific European regulatory and organisational structures may not transfer directly.
takeaways: Identify which digital competencies (e.g. data literacy, cybersecurity awareness, digital tool proficiency) are most critical for your health workforce and prioritise training accordingly.
Use the competency framework as a diagnostic tool to audit gaps in your team's AI and digital capabilities, then design targeted upskilling programs around identified weaknesses.
Align competency development with your organisation's digital transformation roadmap to ensure AI literacy initiatives support strategic goals, not operate in isolation.

articles.title: Mind the gap: an evidence gap analysis of digital literacy within public health systems in the European Union using two different frameworks - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Mind the gap: an evidence gap analysis of digital literacy within public health systems in the European Union using two different frameworks  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focuses specifically on public health systems within EU member states; findings may not generalise to private healthcare sectors, non-EU countries, or other industries, though digital literacy challenges identified may have broader relevance.
takeaways: Use evidence gap analysis frameworks to identify where digital literacy training is most urgently needed in your organisation — this structured approach can help prioritise limited resources toward high-impact interventions.

The EU-specific policy context (GDPR, digital health directives) may differ from Australian regulations; however, the methodological approach of mapping literacy gaps across organisational levels could be adapted to Australian health systems.

articles.title: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education - Nature
articles.snippet: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education  Nature
articles.generalisability: Limited — focuses on middle school education context; applicability to adult workplace AI literacy development requires adaptation. Geographic scope not specified in snippet.
takeaways: Design AI literacy curricula as part of broader digital literacy frameworks rather than isolated modules — this holistic approach better prepares learners to contextualise AI within their existing digital skillsets.

Identify core AI competencies (e.g., understanding algorithmic bias, data concepts, responsible AI use) that should be embedded across subjects rather than taught as standalone content — supports deeper understanding and transfer to work contexts.

articles.title: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health - Frontiers
articles.snippet: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — focuses on faculty development in public health education settings; findings may not transfer directly to corporate workforce development or other sectors without adaptation.
takeaways: Design faculty development programs that address resistance to AI by building confidence and competence incrementally, rather than assuming readiness exists — this parallels change management principles applicable to any organisation introducing AI capabilities.

Position AI literacy as a foundational skill for educators to model and teach, recognising that faculty capability directly influences how effectively learners develop AI competence in their own practice.

Create structured pathways that move participants from resistance to readiness through hands-on, contextualised learning — applicable to designing AI upskilling programs for any professional audience.

articles.title: Data literacy in the labor market: a systematic review | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: Data literacy in the labor market: a systematic review | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate to high — systematic review approach suggests broad geographic scope, though specific country/sector representation depends on included studies (not detailed in snippet).
takeaways: Data literacy is increasingly a foundational workplace skill; audit your organisation's current data literacy levels across roles to identify capability gaps before AI adoption accelerates.

Consider designing tiered data literacy programs (basic numeracy and data interpretation for all; advanced analytics for technical roles) rather than one-size-fits-all training, as labour market demand appears segmented.
Data literacy gaps may compound inequality — monitor who is and isn't gaining data skills in your workforce to avoid creating a two-tier system of AI-capable and AI-dependent employees.

articles.title: AI literacy as a meta-skill: a four-domain model for academic management innovation in higher education - Frontiers
articles.snippet: AI literacy as a meta-skill: a four-domain model for academic management innovation in higher education  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focuses specifically on higher education sector and academic management contexts; applicability to corporate training and non-academic organisations may require adaptation.
takeaways: Use a four-domain framework to structure AI literacy programmes: consider which domains (likely conceptual, technical, ethical, and organisational) your team needs to develop based on their roles and responsibilities.

Position AI literacy as a meta-skill that enables learning of other capabilities rather than a standalone technical skill — this helps justify investment in foundational AI understanding across diverse staff roles.
Design AI literacy interventions differently for academic managers versus technical staff, as the meta-skill approach suggests different domains matter for different roles in driving innovation.

topics.label: AI & Organisational Psychology
topics.description: Impact of AI on wellbeing, engagement, job crafting, trust, and other org psych constructs.

articles.title: The double-edged mechanism of organizational AI adoption on employee creativity - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The double-edged mechanism of organizational AI adoption on employee creativity  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Cannot be fully assessed from title and snippet alone. Generalisability will depend on the study's sample size, industry sectors, geographic locations, and methodological approach — details not evident from the provided information.
takeaways: AI adoption in organisations may have contrasting effects on creativity depending on implementation context; understanding these opposing mechanisms can help leaders design adoption strategies that amplify creative benefits while mitigating constraints.

When planning AI capability development for your team, consider whether the tools are positioned as creativity enablers (e.g., handling routine tasks to free cognitive space) versus creativity replacements (e.g., automating ideation roles), as framing significantly influences employee creative output.

articles.title: Work autonomy mediates associations between medical AI readiness and well being in a three wave nurse study - Nature
articles.snippet: Work autonomy mediates associations between medical AI readiness and well being in a three wave nurse study  Nature
articles.generalisability: Findings are specific to nursing contexts and may not generalise to other professions or sectors. The three-wave design strengthens causal inference but geographic scope is unclear from the snippet.
takeaways: Design AI implementation approaches that preserve or enhance nurses' autonomy and decision-making control — loss of autonomy appears to be the mechanism linking AI readiness to reduced wellbeing.
Use work autonomy as a key metric when assessing whether AI adoption is supporting or undermining staff wellbeing; measure this alongside AI readiness in your own workforce.

During AI rollout, explicitly communicate how AI tools will support rather than replace clinical judgement, and involve frontline staff in designing workflows that maintain their agency in patient care decisions.

articles.title: Competing strain and resource pathways linking AI-enabled work systems to employee wellbeing - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Competing strain and resource pathways linking AI-enabled work systems to employee wellbeing  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on study design and sample composition, which are not detailed in the snippet. Without information on participant demographics, organisational sectors, or geographic scope, applicability to Australian workplace contexts cannot be assessed.
takeaways: AI-enabled work systems can create both positive (resource) and negative (strain) pathways affecting employee wellbeing — organisations should assess which pathway dominates in their context and intervene accordingly.

Understanding competing strain versus resource effects helps tailor AI implementation: focus on maximising autonomy, skill development, and support (resource pathways) while minimising cognitive overload, job insecurity, and loss of control (strain pathways).
Employee wellbeing outcomes from AI adoption are not automatic — deliberate design and change management practices are needed to tip the balance toward resource pathways and away from strain.

articles.title: Dual pathways of generative AI use: role ambiguity and self-efficacy in employee-AI collaboration - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Dual pathways of generative AI use: role ambiguity and self-efficacy in employee-AI collaboration  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear without seeing full methodology. Findings on role ambiguity and self-efficacy in AI collaboration may vary significantly depending on sector, organisational maturity, and employee demographics. Frontiers publications are peer-reviewed but sample characteristics and geographic scope are not evident from title alone.
takeaways: Role ambiguity—uncertainty about how AI should fit into job responsibilities—is a key barrier to effective employee-AI collaboration; clarifying AI-related role expectations may be more impactful than technical training alone.

Self-efficacy (confidence in one's ability to use AI effectively) appears to be a modifiable lever; investing in structured opportunities for small wins and competence-building with AI tools can unlock adoption regardless of initial anxiety.

Addressing both pathways simultaneously—reducing role confusion while building confidence—likely yields better outcomes than focusing on either technical capability or organisational clarity in isolation.

articles.title: When AI works, employees worry: the vigilance cost of AI delegation in hybrid work - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When AI works, employees worry: the vigilance cost of AI delegation in hybrid work  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Cannot fully assess without access to full article. Title and snippet suggest a focused study on hybrid work contexts; findings may be specific to particular industries or role types where AI delegation occurs.
takeaways: When delegating tasks to AI systems, employees may experience increased cognitive load from monitoring and verifying outputs rather than decreased workload — factor this 'vigilance cost' into AI adoption planning, especially for hybrid teams.

Hybrid work environments may amplify anxiety about AI delegation due to reduced social cues and informal oversight — consider implementing clear accountability structures and verification protocols when introducing AI tools to distributed teams.

Design AI workflows that minimise unnecessary monitoring burden by providing clear confidence scores, audit trails, or exception-based alerts so employees don't default to exhausting manual verification.

articles.title: Workers are facing an age of uncertainty - American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.snippet: Workers are facing an age of uncertainty  American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.generalisability: US-focused findings from APA; workplace uncertainty themes may resonate internationally, but specific data on US workforce context may not transfer directly to Australian employment settings.
takeaways: Acknowledge and name uncertainty as a legitimate workplace stressor when introducing AI capabilities — employees may benefit from transparent communication about how roles will evolve rather than reassurance alone.

Create structured opportunities for employees to voice concerns about change and job security; psychological safety around these conversations can reduce anxiety and improve engagement with AI upskilling initiatives.
Monitor wellbeing indicators (stress, engagement, retention) alongside AI adoption metrics — uncertainty's psychological toll may undermine capability development if not actively managed.

topics.label: Behavioural Change Frameworks
topics.description: Evidence-based frameworks for driving behaviour change — in the context of AI adoption and workforce transformation.

articles.title: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI - Deloitte
articles.snippet: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI  Deloitte
articles.generalisability: Moderate — Deloitte's framework is based on consulting experience across multiple sectors, but specific client examples and geographic scope are not detailed in the snippet. Applicability to Australian organisations will depend on alignment with local workplace culture and regulatory context.
takeaways: Shift from 'AI adoption' framing to 'AI adaptation' — focus change management on building new human behaviours and ways of working rather than simply rolling out technology.

Design change initiatives that explicitly target the behavioural shifts required for AI success (e.g., comfort with ambiguity, data literacy, collaboration with AI systems) rather than treating behaviour change as secondary to implementation.
Use a human-centred change approach that identifies and reinforces the specific capabilities and mindsets your workforce needs to work effectively alongside AI tools.

articles.title: Dual-path mechanism of AI awareness on employee job crafting: insights from the cognitive appraisal of stress and JD-R perspective | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: Dual-path mechanism of AI awareness on employee job crafting: insights from the cognitive appraisal of stress and JD-R perspective | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample characteristics not evident from the title and snippet. The study applies established psychological frameworks (cognitive appraisal theory and Job Demands-Resources model) which have broad applicability, but limitations would depend on the specific sample size, sector, and geographic scope — information not provided in the snippet.
takeaways: AI awareness can trigger two distinct pathways in how employees reshape their roles: one through stress appraisal (viewing AI as threatening) and another through the demands-resources framework. Understanding which pathway is activated for your team helps tailor support — some may need reassurance about job security, while others need clarity on how AI creates new opportunities.

Job crafting (how employees proactively modify their tasks and responsibilities) may be a mechanism through which employees adapt to AI introduction. Encouraging deliberate conversation about how roles can evolve with AI tools — rather than waiting for anxiety to drive change — could help employees take agency earlier in the transition.

articles.title: How AI Is Reshaping the Future of Work - Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.snippet: How AI Is Reshaping the Future of Work  Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to be a Stanford GSB perspective piece without specified empirical data, sample, or geographic scope. Findings may reflect US higher education and business school viewpoints rather than broader workforce patterns.
takeaways: Identify specific AI-driven work transitions in your organisation and design targeted upskilling programs before roles shift, rather than reactive retraining after disruption occurs.

Create forums where employees can experiment with AI tools in low-stakes settings to build confidence and reduce anxiety about technological change — this psychological safety approach is often more effective than top-down mandate-style adoption.
Map which of your employees face highest disruption risk and prioritise them for early involvement in change initiatives, as proactive engagement reduces resistance and improves transition outcomes.

articles.title: Are all digital hoarding behavior alike? Uncovering the pathways to digital hoarding behavior in the workplace - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Are all digital hoarding behavior alike? Uncovering the pathways to digital hoarding behavior in the workplace  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — snippet does not clarify geographic scope, sample size, or sector. Findings may be specific to the organisational context(s) studied and may not generalise broadly across different workplace cultures or industries.
takeaways: Digital hoarding (excessive file/email retention) has multiple distinct psychological or behavioural drivers in workplace settings — understanding which pathway an employee follows (e.g., perfectionism, anxiety, organisational culture) is necessary before designing targeted interventions.

Generic 'declutter your digital workspace' campaigns are unlikely to work; behaviour-change strategies should be tailored to the underlying cause of hoarding behaviour in your specific team or organisation.

articles.title: From adoption to impact: Three horizons of AI transformation - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: From adoption to impact: Three horizons of AI transformation  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — based on McKinsey's client work and industry observations, likely skewed toward large enterprises and developed economies. Specific findings may not generalise to small-to-medium businesses or resource-constrained organisations.
takeaways: Map your organisation's AI maturity across three distinct phases (adoption, scaling, sustained impact) to identify which stage requires immediate attention and what capabilities need building next.
Recognise that moving from AI pilots to organisational impact requires deliberate behaviour change — shifting how teams work, make decisions, and measure success, not just deploying technology.

Identify and address the 'valley of death' between early adoption and sustained impact, where many organisations stall; this requires sustained leadership commitment and cultural reinforcement, not one-off training.

articles.title: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear from snippet alone — depends on sample size, sector diversity, and geographic scope of the study, which are not evident from the title and abstract provided.
takeaways: Job crafting behaviours (how employees reshape their role) can be influenced by how they perceive AI adoption — understanding whether staff view AI as a threat to avoid or an opportunity to approach is key to shaping adoption outcomes.

Organisational psychologists can design AI implementation strategies that reframe AI adoption through an 'approach' lens (focusing on skill development and role expansion) rather than an 'avoidance' lens (fear of displacement), to encourage proactive job crafting rather than defensive withdrawal.

Monitor and assess employee motivation patterns during AI rollout — those using avoidance coping may disengage from upskilling or role adaptation, so early intervention to build psychological safety around AI is critical for positive behaviour change.

topics.label: Fascinating Psychology Research
topics.description: Surprising, counterintuitive, and delightful findings from personality and behaviour research — the kind of study you'd share at dinner.

articles.title: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people - Science Daily
articles.snippet: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people  Science Daily
articles.generalisability: Unable to assess without access to full article — 'shocking difference' claims in neuroscience headlines often overstate findings from small or specialised samples.
takeaways: Brain imaging studies on psychopathy often rely on incarcerated or clinical populations, which may not represent the full spectrum of psychopathic traits in the general population.
The headline framing ('shocking difference') is typical of science communication that emphasises novelty — the actual neurobiological findings may be more nuanced than implied.
Psychopathy exists on a continuum rather than as a binary category, so any brain scan 'difference' likely reflects degrees rather than a clear-cut divide between two distinct groups.

articles.title: New psychology research shows the surprising romantic advantage of antagonistic narcissism - PsyPost
articles.snippet: New psychology research shows the surprising romantic advantage of antagonistic narcissism  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Not determinable from snippet — no details on study design, sample size, or geographic scope provided.
takeaways: Antagonistic narcissism (dominance-seeking, callous traits) appears to confer short-term romantic appeal, suggesting some narcissistic behaviours can be attractive despite their interpersonal toxicity.

The finding inverts the stereotype that narcissism is universally repellent romantically — it hints that grandiosity and assertiveness may trigger attraction even when coupled with emotional coldness.

This reveals a mismatch between what makes someone initially appealing and what makes relationships actually work, raising questions about whether evolutionary mating psychology sometimes rewards traits that harm long-term partnership quality.

articles.title: When personality meets surprise: individual differences in memory for unexpected events - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When personality meets surprise: individual differences in memory for unexpected events  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on the study's sample composition and size; without access to the full article, limitations around participant demographics, cultural context, and whether findings hold across different types of unexpected events remain unclear.
takeaways: People with different personality types don't all remember surprising moments the same way — some personalities appear to encode unexpected events more vividly than others, challenging the assumption that shock creates uniform memory in everyone.

Your personality isn't just about how you behave; it fundamentally shapes what your brain decides to lock into memory when something catches you off guard — a surprising link between 'who you are' and 'what you remember'.

articles.title: How a twin study untangled the surprising roots of authoritarian political beliefs - PsyPost
articles.snippet: How a twin study untangled the surprising roots of authoritarian political beliefs  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet alone — twin studies can provide insights into nature/nurture contributions to traits, but generalisability depends on sample composition, country of origin, and how authoritarianism was measured. Limited by the snapshot nature of twin methodology.
takeaways: Authoritarian political beliefs appear to have a heritable genetic component, not just environmental roots — suggesting personality traits linked to authoritarianism run in families for nature-based reasons, not just shared upbringing.

This finding is counterintuitive because political ideology is often assumed to be entirely learned through family socialisation and lived experience, when twin studies reveal biology plays a measurable role.

The result highlights why political disagreement within families can be so stubborn — if genetic predispositions influence authoritarianism, people literally approach hierarchy and obedience differently at a biological level.

articles.title: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe - University of Cambridge
articles.snippet: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe  University of Cambridge
articles.generalisability: High — findings suggest cross-cultural consistency in how music preferences relate to personality, though specific music genres and cultural contexts may vary by region.
takeaways: Your taste in music is a surprisingly reliable window into your personality — people with similar personality traits gravitate toward the same genres worldwide, suggesting personality shapes what we listen to more than culture alone does.

This connection between personality and music preference holds across wildly different cultures, hinting that something universal about human psychology links how we think and feel to the sounds we enjoy.
If you want a quick read on someone's personality, their Spotify playlist might tell you as much as a formal assessment — which is both fascinating and a bit unsettling.

articles.title: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality - PsyPost
articles.snippet: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet — sample size, geographic scope, and methodology are not detailed. Generalisability depends on whether the wine review dataset is representative across cultures and wine-drinking populations.
takeaways: Language patterns in how people describe wine reveal personality traits — an unexpected window into character that has nothing to do with the wine itself.
AI can detect personality signals hidden in everyday writing, suggesting our word choices betray more about who we are than we realise.
Wine reviews, a seemingly trivial form of consumer commentary, turned out to be surprisingly rich data for understanding human personality.

topics.label: Psychological Safety
topics.description: Research on psychological safety and its role in team learning, AI experimentation, and innovation.

articles.title: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2026 - PwC
articles.snippet: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2026  PwC
articles.generalisability: Broad global reach, though likely skewed toward larger organisations and developed economies where PwC operates. Sample composition and methodology not detailed in snippet, limiting assessment of representativeness across sectors and geographies.
takeaways: Use employee sentiment data from large-scale surveys to identify psychological safety gaps in your organisation — compare your team's concerns against global workforce trends to prioritise interventions.

When designing safety-focused initiatives, anchor messaging to employees' actual hopes and fears rather than assumed concerns — this PwC data can help validate whether your assumptions about what matters to staff align with broader workforce sentiment.

articles.title: When inclusive leadership promotes innovation: the role of team psychological safety and leader power distance orientation - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When inclusive leadership promotes innovation: the role of team psychological safety and leader power distance orientation  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — findings depend on the specific sample characteristics (size, sectors, countries) not evident from title and snippet. The relationship between inclusive leadership, psychological safety, and innovation may vary across organisational cultures and national contexts with different power distance norms.
takeaways: Leaders who adopt inclusive practices and maintain lower power distance (encourage input from all levels) create stronger team psychological safety, which directly enables innovation — audit your own leadership style for barriers to voice and participation.

Psychological safety acts as a mechanism linking inclusive leadership to innovation outcomes — if your team isn't generating novel ideas despite inclusive practices, investigate whether team members actually feel safe to speak up and challenge the status quo without fear of embarrassment or punishment.

articles.title: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample composition — unclear from snippet whether findings are limited to specific sectors, countries, or organisation types. The theoretical pathway (AI adoption → reduced psychological safety → depression) may vary significantly across different workplace cultures and implementation contexts.
takeaways: Monitor psychological safety closely during AI adoption rollouts; reduced sense of safety and autonomy can become a hidden cost of implementation that manifests in employee mental health — look for early warning signs in team feedback and engagement metrics.

Ethical leadership becomes critical when introducing AI — transparent communication about AI's role, why roles are changing, and how decisions are made can buffer against the negative psychological impact of adoption.
Don't treat AI adoption as purely a technical change; frame it as an organisational intervention that requires attention to psychological wellbeing, not just capability upskilling.

articles.title: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG report likely draws on global consulting experience, but specific sample details, sectors, and research methodology are not evident from the title and snippet alone. Findings may reflect practices most visible to large multinational organisations.
takeaways: Psychological safety can reduce performance inequalities across employee demographics by creating conditions where all team members feel confident contributing ideas without fear of embarrassment or retaliation.
Leaders can use psychological safety as a strategic lever to unlock participation and engagement from employees who might otherwise self-censor due to social or organisational barriers.
Measuring and monitoring psychological safety climate within teams can help identify where participation gaps exist and target interventions to build more inclusive team dynamics.

articles.title: Reframing workplace safety, wellbeing, and performance among operating room nurses in contemporary healthcare systems - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Reframing workplace safety, wellbeing, and performance among operating room nurses in contemporary healthcare systems  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to focus on operating room nursing context; generalisability to other healthcare roles or non-healthcare sectors unclear without access to full methodology.
takeaways: Operating room environments require integrated approaches linking psychological safety to both staff wellbeing and clinical performance outcomes — consider how your organisation measures and reinforces these connections in high-stakes settings.

Reframing safety narratives from compliance-focused to holistic wellbeing-and-performance models may improve staff engagement; audit whether your current safety messaging addresses psychological safety alongside physical and operational safety.

articles.title: Human capabilities are at the heart of high-performing teams - Deloitte
articles.snippet: Human capabilities are at the heart of high-performing teams  Deloitte
articles.generalisability: Limited — Deloitte report likely draws on client experience and consulting practice, but specific methodology, sample size, and geographic scope are unclear from the snippet. Findings may reflect Deloitte's client base rather than broader workforce populations.
takeaways: Prioritise capability development and human skills alongside structural interventions when building high-performing teams — technical processes alone are insufficient without attention to how people interact and collaborate.

Psychological safety enables teams to develop and deploy human capabilities effectively; assess whether your team environment allows people to speak up, take interpersonal risks, and learn from mistakes without fear of embarrassment or retaliation.
